hook: Alexey Kurakin built an early research career studying pattern recognition and hand gesture recognition before moving into deep learning. At Google he became one of the first researchers to show that adversarial examples, inputs deliberately perturbed to fool machine learning models, remain effective even after being printed and photographed with a camera, publishing this result with Ian Goodfellow and Samy Bengio as Adversarial Examples in the Physical World. The same period he co-authored Adversarial Machine Learning at Scale, studying how adversarial training could be applied to large image classifiers. In 2016 he demonstrated a physical adversarial attack live at the GeekPwn security conference alongside Ian Goodfellow. He later broadened his research to semi-supervised learning, co-authoring methods including FixMatch, ReMixMatch, and AdaMatch, and continues to work as a research scientist at Google.
name: Alexey Kurakin
moniker: Researcher in adversarial machine learning and robustness

reading.body:
Adversarial examples—inputs deliberately perturbed to fool machine learning models—remain effective even after being printed and photographed, establishing that robustness failures are a physical security concern, not merely a digital one.

Kurakin's early work with Goodfellow and Bengio moved adversarial machine learning beyond the laboratory. By showing that attacks survive the analog journey from screen to paper to camera, they revealed that deployed models face real-world vulnerability. This matters because any system relying on visual input—from autonomous vehicles to industrial inspection—inherits this fragility. The work established that robustness is not a theoretical edge case but a practical requirement for safety-critical applications.

His later research on adversarial training at scale and semi-supervised learning methods like FixMatch address a related constraint: the cost of labeling data. As models grow larger and compute demands increase, the human labor required to generate training labels becomes a bottleneck. Semi-supervised techniques that reduce this dependency make efficient scaling possible. This work does not directly address power or infrastructure, but it bears on how efficiently organizations can prepare data pipelines to feed growing computational capacity.

The data covers Kurakin's published research and employer but provides no information about his influence on model deployment decisions, industry adoption of his methods, or changes to safety practices following his demonstrations.
